1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, and bounded
10	  `loop` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
30	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
31	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
32	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
33	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
34	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
35	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
36	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
37	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
38	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
39	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
40	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
41	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
42	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
43	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
44	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
45	  resumed, and periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
46	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy.
47	
48	## Requirements
49	
50	- Python 3.11 or newer
51	- no third-party runtime dependencies
52	
53	## Run the service
54	
55	```bash
56	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
57	```
58	
59	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
60	has bound the port.
61	
62	## HTTP API
63	
64	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
65	
66	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
67	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
68	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
69	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
70	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
71	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
72	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
73	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
74	
75	### Tenants and quotas
76	
77	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
78	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
79	and delivery history record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
80	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
81	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
82	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
83	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
84	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, or schedule of an execution or
85	workflow owned by another tenant — is answered exactly like a reference to a
86	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
87	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
88	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
89	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
90	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
91	
92	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
93	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
94	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, and all history and status
95	queries, as well as the usage, bill, and metrics queries. An empty
96	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
97	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
98	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
99	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
100	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
101	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
102	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
103	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
104	the usual `409 conflict`.
105	
106	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
107	hold:
108	
109	```http
110	PUT /quotas
111	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
112	X-Tenant-Id: acme
113	
114	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
115	```
116	
117	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
118	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
119	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
120	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
121	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
122	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
123	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
124	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
125	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
126	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
127	
128	```http
129	GET /quotas
130	X-Tenant-Id: acme
131	```
132	
133	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
134	when the tenant has declared none.
135	
136	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
137	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
138	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
139	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
140	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
141	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
142	
143	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
144	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
145	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
146	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
147	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
148	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
149	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
150	
151	### Usage metering and billing
152	
153	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
154	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
155	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
156	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
157	metered action types are:
158	
159	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
160	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
161	  definition;
162	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
163	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
164	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
165	  `schedule_triggered`;
166	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made. A
167	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
168	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
169	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails.
170	
171	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
172	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
173	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
174	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
175	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
176	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
177	
178	```http
179	GET /usage
180	X-Tenant-Id: acme
181	```
182	
183	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
184	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
185	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
186	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
187	
188	```http
189	GET /bill
190	X-Tenant-Id: acme
191	```
192	
193	Returns the per-type bill:
194	
195	```json
196	{"bill":{"items":[
197	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
198	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
199	],"total":2100}}
200	```
201	
202	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
203	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
204	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
205	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`.
206	
207	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
208	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`. Usage and bill data follow the
209	usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see another's records.
210	
211	### Operational metrics
212	
213	```http
214	GET /metrics
215	X-Tenant-Id: acme
216	```
217	
218	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
219	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
220	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
221	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
222	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
223	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
224	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
225	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
226	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
227	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
228	every dimension at zero — not an error.
229	
230	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
231	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
232	failures, and schedule triggers:
233	
234	```json
235	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
236	```
237	
238	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
239	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
240	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
241	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
242	  ended for that reason.
243	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
244	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
245	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
246	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
247	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
248	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
249	  another attempt, per node identifier.
250	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
251	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
252	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
253	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
254	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
255	
256	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
257	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
258	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
259	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
260	the migration accumulate under the same names. Filtering by time range and
261	export formats are out of scope.

263	### Health
264	
265	```http
266	GET /health
267	```
268	
269	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.

271	### Create a workflow
272	
273	```http
274	POST /workflows
275	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
276	
277	{
278	  "id": "order-flow",
279	  "nodes": [
280	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
281	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
282	  ]
283	}
284	```
285	
286	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
287	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
288	
289	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
290	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
291	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
292	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
293	
294	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
295	
296	```json
297	{
298	  "id": "order-flow",
299	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
300	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
301	}
302	```
303	
304	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
305	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
306	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
307	
308	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
309	
310	```json
311	{
312	  "id": "nightly-orders",
313	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
314	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
315	}
316	```
317	
318	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
319	
320	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
321	
322	```json
323	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
324	```
325	
326	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
327	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
328	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
329	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
330	`false`.
331	
332	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
333	
334	```json
335	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
336	```
337	
338	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
339	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
340	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
341	dependencies of its successors.
342	
343	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
344	
345	```json
346	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
347	```
348	
349	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
350	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
351	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
352	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
353	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
354	`retries_exhausted`.
355	
356	A task may instead declare an approval point:
357	
358	```json
359	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
360	```
361	
362	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
363	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
364	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
365	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
366	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
367	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
368	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
369	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
370	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
371	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
372	move the task.
373	
374	### Submit an approval decision
375	
376	```http
377	POST /executions/run-1/decision
378	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
379	
380	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
381	```
382	
383	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
384	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
385	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
386	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
387	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
388	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
389	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
390	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
391	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
392	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
393	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
394	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
395	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
396	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
397	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
398	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
399	404.
400	
401	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
402	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
403	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
404	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
405	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
406	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
407	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
408	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
409	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
410	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
411	shape and event stream.
412	
413	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
414	segment:
415	
416	```json
417	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
418	```
419	
420	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
421	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
422	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
423	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
424	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
425	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
426	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
427	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
428	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
429	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
430	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
431	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
432	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
433	loop node instead).
434	
435	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
436	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
437	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
438	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
439	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
440	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
441	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
442	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
443	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
444	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
445	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
446	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
447	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
448	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
449	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
450	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
451	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
452	belong only to their iterations.
453	
454	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
455	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
456	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
457	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
458	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
459	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
460	exactly.
461	
462	### Workflow versions
463	
464	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
465	
466	```json
467	{
468	  "id": "order-flow",
469	  "version": "2026-09-25",
470	  "nodes": [
471	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
472	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
473	  ]
474	}
475	```
476	
477	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
478	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
479	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
480	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
481	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
482	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
483	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
484	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
485	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
486	
487	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
488	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
489	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
490	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
491	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
492	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
493	
494	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
495	current version at the moment it starts:
496	
497	```http
498	POST /executions
499	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
500	
501	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
502	```
503	
504	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
505	
506	```json
507	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
508	```
509	
510	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
511	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
512	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
513	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
514	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
515	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
516	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
517	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
518	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
519	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
520	conclusions never change.
521	
522	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
523	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
524	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
525	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
526	stream with no added field.
527	
528	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
529	
530	```http
531	GET /workflows/order-flow
532	```
533	
534	```json
535	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
536	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
537	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
538	]}
539	```
540	
541	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
542	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
543	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
544	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
545	resources as usual.
546	
547	### Migrate a running execution to another version
548	
549	```http
550	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
551	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
552	
553	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
554	```
555	
556	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
557	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
558	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
559	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
560	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
561	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
562	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
563	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
564	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
565	carries the target version.
566	
567	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
568	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
569	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
570	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
571	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
572	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
573	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
574	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
575	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
576	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
577	
578	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
579	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
580	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
581	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
582	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
583	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
584	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
585	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
586	content.
587	
588	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
589	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
590	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
591	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
592	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
593	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
594	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
595	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
596	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
597	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
598	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
599	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
600	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
601	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.
602	
603	### Start an execution
604	
605	```http
606	POST /executions
607	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
608	
609	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
610	```
611	
612	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
613	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
614	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
615	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
616	
617	An execution may declare a timeout:
618	
619	```json
620	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
621	```
622	
623	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
624	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
625	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
626	a timeout never expire.
627	
628	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
629	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
630	
631	```json
632	{
633	  "id": "run-3",
634	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
635	  "input": {},
636	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
637	}
638	```
639	
640	### Inspect an execution
641	
642	```http
643	GET /executions/run-1
644	GET /executions/run-1/events
645	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
646	```
647	
648	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
649	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
650	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
651	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
652	
653	### Webhook notifications
654	
655	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
656	messages when business events occur. Each subscription contains exactly:
657	
658	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
659	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
660	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
661	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
662	  reason);
663	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
664	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
665	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
666	
667	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
668	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
669	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
670	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
671	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written.
672	
673	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
674	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
675	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
676	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
677	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
678	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
679	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
680	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
681	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
682	triggered it.
683	
684	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
685	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
686	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
687	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
688	results as before.
689	
690	### Inspect the delivery history
691	
692	```http
693	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
694	```
695	
696	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
697	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
698	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
699	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
700	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
701	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
702	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
703	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
704	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
705	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
706	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
707	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
708	
709	### Schedules
710	
711	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
712	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
713	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
714	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
715	
716	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
717	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
718	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
719	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
720	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
721	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
722	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
723	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
724	
725	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
726	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
727	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
728	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
729	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
730	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
731	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
732	created is exposed through the status query below.
733	
734	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
735	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
736	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
737	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
738	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
739	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
740	
741	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
742	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
743	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
744	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
745	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
746	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
747	
748	### Declare or replace a schedule
749	
750	```http
751	PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
752	Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1
753	
754	{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
755	```
756	
757	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
758	like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
759	status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
760	paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
761	plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
762	idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.
763	
764	### Inspect the schedule status
765	
766	```http
767	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
768	```
769	
770	Returns a single `schedule` object with the status fields, or the definite
771	empty result `{"schedule":null}` for a workflow that never declared a
772	schedule. When a schedule exists the object is:
773	
774	```json
775	{
776	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"},
777	  "paused": false,
778	  "last_triggered_at": "2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z",
779	  "last_execution_id": "nightly-orders-scheduled-i:42"
780	}
781	```
782	
783	The fields are:
784	
785	- `schedule`: the declared plan exactly as stored — either
786	  `{"interval_seconds": <positive integer>, "input": <object>, "missed_policy": "catch_up"|"skip"}`
787	  or `{"cron": "<five-field expression>", "input": <object>, "missed_policy": ...}`;
788	  the input is the declared object verbatim;
789	- `paused`: a JSON boolean;
790	- `last_triggered_at`: an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp string ending in `Z`, or
791	  `null` until the first period fires;
792	- `last_execution_id`: the execution id string of the most recently created
793	  run, or `null` until the first trigger.
794	
795	`last_triggered_at` and `last_execution_id` are `null` (not omitted) until
796	the first trigger. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.
797	
798	### Pause and resume a schedule
799	
800	```http
801	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
802	Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1
803	
804	{}
805	```
806	
807	```http
808	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
809	Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1
810	
811	{}
812	```
813	
814	Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
815	field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
816	periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
817	during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
818	creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
819	resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
820	missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
821	operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.
822	
823	Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
824	advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
825	exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.
826	
827	### Checkpoints
828	
829	Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
830	completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
831	attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
832	and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
833	boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
834	outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
835	current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
836	with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
837	the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
838	duplicating any node output.
839	
840	Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
841	an execution that declares no retries, timeout, or loops keeps exactly the
842	same state shape and event stream as before.
843	
844	### Complete the next ready node
845	
846	```http
847	POST /executions/run-1/advance
848	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-1
849	
850	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"}}
851	```
852	
853	The lexicographically first ready task is completed. The response contains the
854	updated execution. Before that, each call first evaluates all ready conditions
855	in deterministic order and skips tasks whose `run_if` does not match; if this
856	automatic processing finishes the execution, the current state is returned and
857	the submitted output is not consumed. When every node is completed or skipped,
858	the status becomes `completed`.
859	
860	Instead of an output, a failure can be submitted for the same ready task:
861	
862	```http
863	POST /executions/run-1/advance
864	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-2
865	
866	{"failure":{"reason":"gateway timeout"}}
867	```
868	
869	The body must contain exactly one of `output` or `failure`, and `failure`
870	carries exactly a `reason` string. Either body may additionally carry a
871	`worker_id` string identifying the lease holder when the execution's work
872	item has been claimed (see "Claim a work item"). A failed task appends a `node_failed`
873	event recording the attempt number and reason. While the task has retries
874	left it returns to the ready set and a `node_retried` event records the next
875	attempt number; otherwise the task is permanently failed and the execution
876	terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`. The same rules apply to tasks
877	inside loop bodies, which are retried within their current iteration.
878	
879	Execution state includes `completed_nodes` (which also lists evaluated
880	conditions), `skipped_nodes`, `failed_nodes`, `condition_results`, `outputs`,
881	and `attempts`. `attempts` maps each attempted task to its current `attempt`
882	number and its `failures` count; loop body tasks track the same per iteration.
883	Executions of workflows that declare approval points additionally expose
884	`waiting_approval` (`null`, or the pending point's `node_id`, `approvers`, and
885	loop context) and the `approvals` record list. Each condition evaluation
886	appends a `condition_evaluated` event and each skip a `node_skipped` event to
887	the execution stream.
888	
889	### Cancel an execution
890	
891	```http
892	POST /executions/run-1/cancel
893	Idempotency-Key: cancel-request-1
894	```
895	
896	A running execution is terminated immediately with termination reason
897	`cancelled`. Cancelling a completed or already terminated execution returns
898	its state unchanged, and cancelling a missing execution returns 404.
899	
900	Execution status is `running`, `completed`, or `terminated`. A terminated
901	execution records exactly one `termination_reason` — `retries_exhausted`,
902	`rejected`, `timeout`, or `cancelled` — and appends a single
903	`execution_terminated` event; completed executions keep a `null` termination
904	reason and their own `execution_completed` event. Advancing a terminated
905	execution returns its state unchanged without consuming the submitted output
906	or failure; a decision against one only succeeds as a repeat of the decision
907	that rejected it, and otherwise conflicts.
908	
909	### Claim a work item
910	
911	```http
912	POST /executions/run-1/claim
913	Idempotency-Key: claim-request-1
914	
915	{"worker_id":"worker-7","lease_seconds":30}
916	```
917	
918	Claiming is how an external worker takes ownership of a running execution
919	before advancing its ready tasks. `worker_id` is a non-empty string and
920	`lease_seconds` is an optional positive number of seconds (default 30). The
921	response contains the claimed `work_item` (its `execution_id` and
922	`workflow_id`) and a `lease` recording the `worker_id`, the `lease_seconds`
923	duration, the `expires_at` deadline, and the `heartbeat_at` active time.
924	Each work item is held by at most one worker at a time: claiming a work
925	item whose lease is still active — even by the same worker — is a 409
926	`conflict`. Claiming a completed or terminated execution returns the
927	definite empty result `{"work_item":null,"lease":null}` and absorbs no
928	input, and claiming a missing execution returns 404.
929	
930	While a work item is held, results are submitted through the usual
931	`advance` entry by including the holder's identity:
932	
933	```http
934	POST /executions/run-1/advance
935	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-3
936	
937	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"},"worker_id":"worker-7"}
938	```
939	
940	Submitting results for a work item held by another worker, or after the
941	lease has expired, is a 409 `conflict` that does not change execution
942	state. An execution that never claimed a work item accepts `advance`
943	exactly as before, and its state fields and event stream are identical to
944	an execution without any claim.
945	
946	When a lease expires, the work item returns to the claimable set and may be
947	claimed again by the same or another worker. The second claim continues
948	from the materialized state: node outputs and results recorded by the
949	earlier holder are never advanced or recorded twice, and every written
950	output belongs to the single advance that submitted it.
951	
952	### Renew a lease
953	
954	```http
955	POST /executions/run-1/heartbeat
956	Idempotency-Key: heartbeat-request-1
957	
958	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
959	```
960	
961	Within the lease period the holder may heartbeat to extend `expires_at` by
962	the lease duration and refresh the `heartbeat_at` active time; the response
963	carries the updated `lease`. A heartbeat never advances nodes, writes
964	outputs, or appends node events. A heartbeat from another worker or after
965	the lease expired is a 409 `conflict`; a heartbeat for a missing execution
966	or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404 `not_found`.
967	
968	### Release a work item
969	
970	```http
971	POST /executions/run-1/release
972	Idempotency-Key: release-request-1
973	
974	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
975	```
976	
977	Releasing invalidates the lease immediately and returns the work item to
978	the claimable set, so it can be claimed again right away; progress already
979	made and the recorded events are unchanged. Releasing with another
980	worker's identity or after expiry is a 409 `conflict`; releasing for a
981	missing execution or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404
982	`not_found`.
983	
984	Claims, heartbeats, and releases append no events and add no fields to the
985	execution state, so replay, checkpoints, and recovery are unaffected.
986	Leases live in the same SQLite database as the execution state, so
987	unexpired leases and claim ownership remain valid after the service
988	restarts.
989	
990	### Recover from a checkpoint
991	
992	```http
993	POST /executions/run-1/recover
994	Idempotency-Key: recover-request-1
995	
996	{"from":"latest_checkpoint"}
997	```
998	
999	Recovery rebuilds a running execution from its latest checkpoint and returns
1000	the rebuilt execution. It appends no events and changes no state: the rebuilt
1001	execution is exactly the materialized state, and a subsequent replay has the
1002	same conclusion as before the interruption. After recovery, further
1003	`advance` calls continue from the checkpoint, so node outputs, failure
1004	reasons, attempt numbers, and loop iteration ownership are identical to an
1005	uninterrupted run; failure records for tasks inside a loop body still carry
1006	their loop id and current iteration. Recovery works after the service has
1007	been restarted, because checkpoints live in the same SQLite database as the
1008	execution state and events.
1009	
1010	A completed execution is returned unchanged, producing no new events. A
1011	terminated execution is likewise returned unchanged and the operation
1012	absorbs no input; if a timeout or cancellation takes effect between
1013	checkpoint writes, termination takes precedence over recovery. Events and
1014	checkpoints remain queryable after cancellation or timeout, and their replay
1015	stays consistent with the materialized state.
1016	
1017	Recovering a missing execution returns 404. Recovering an execution that has
1018	no checkpoint, or whose latest checkpoint cannot be parsed, returns 409
1019	`conflict`. A missing `from` field, a wrong type, or an unknown recovery
1020	origin is a 400 `validation_error`; a non-finite number in the body is
1021	rejected the same way as every other request. Reusing an idempotency key
1022	already used by another operation (including an `advance` or `cancel` on the
1023	same execution) returns 409 `conflict`.
1024	
1025	### Replay
1026	
1027	```http
1028	POST /executions/run-1/replay
1029	```
1030	
1031	Rebuilds state solely from the execution event stream and compares it with the
1032	stored materialized state. A successful response contains `consistent: true`
1033	and the rebuilt execution.
1034	
1035	## Errors
1036	
1037	Errors use this shape:
1038	
1039	```json
1040	{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"human readable detail"}}
1041	```
1042	
1043	Validation errors return 400, missing resources return 404, and conflicts
1044	return 409. An empty `X-Tenant-Id` header value is a validation error; quota
1045	declarations and the usage, bill, and metrics queries require a tenant, and
1046	quota limits are positive integers validated by the
1047	same rules as every other body (no non-finite numbers, no unknown fields).
1048	Reusing a workflow or execution identifier, adding a workflow version whose
1049	tag already exists for that workflow, or reusing an idempotency key across
1050	different operations (within the same tenant), is a conflict. Starting an
1051	execution against a missing workflow or a missing workflow version is a
1052	missing resource (`404 not_found`). Migrating an execution to a missing
1053	version is likewise a missing resource, while migrating a completed or
1054	terminated execution is a conflict; a malformed migration body is a
1055	validation error, and a migration to the version already bound is a
1056	state-returning no-op rather than an error.
1057	Exceeding a tenant's declared workflow or execution quota is also a `409
1058	conflict`, with the word "quota" in the message so it can be distinguished
1059	from an identifier conflict; the rejected request writes nothing. Referencing
1060	a resource owned by another tenant is a missing resource (`404
1061	not_found`), indistinguishable from one that does not exist, so existence is
1062	never revealed across tenants. A `retries` value that is negative, non-integer, or greater than
1063	10, and a non-positive `timeout_seconds`, are validation errors. A malformed
1064	subscription — a missing or mistyped field, an unknown field, an empty or
1065	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1066	a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than ten attempts — is a
1067	validation error that rejects the whole request without partial writes, and
1068	querying the delivery history of a missing execution is a missing resource. An approval
1069	point with an empty approver list, a duplicate or non-string approver, an
1070	approval on a non-task node, and a decision body that is malformed or carries
1071	a decision other than `approved` or `rejected` are validation errors.
1072	A decision by an approver who is
1073	not listed for the pending point, or any decision against an execution that
1074	has no pending approval point (other than a repeat of the decision that
1075	resolved the latest one), is a conflict. Claiming a work item whose lease is
1076	still active, submitting results for a work item held by another worker or
1077	after the lease expired, and heartbeating or releasing a lease held by
1078	another worker are conflicts, while heartbeating or releasing an execution
1079	with no claimed work item is a missing resource. Recovering a missing
1080	execution is a missing resource, while recovering an execution that has no
1081	checkpoint or whose latest checkpoint is unparseable is a conflict; an
1082	invalid recover body is a validation error. An invalid schedule declaration —
1083	a non-positive or non-integer interval, a malformed or out-of-range cron
1084	expression, declaring both an interval and a cron plan, an unknown missed
1085	policy, or an unknown field — is a validation error that rejects the whole
1086	request without partial writes; pausing, resuming, or updating the schedule
1087	of a missing workflow, or pausing and resuming a workflow that has no
1088	schedule, is a missing resource, and a malformed pause or resume body is a
1089	validation error. Request bodies must not contain
1090	non-finite numbers (`NaN`, `Infinity`, or overflowing values such as `1e400`);
1091	they are rejected with 400. Finite floats keep their full precision, including negative zero
1092	(`-0.0`), and every response body ends with a single newline.
1093	
1094	## Tests
1095	
1096	```bash
1097	PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
1098	```
1099
